objective: Optimizing flow: limiting work in progress at every level, shielding the team from interruptions, and using metrics to keep improving flow

sources.cite: PMI, PMI Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) Examination Content Outline (March 2026): Mindset 28%, Leadership 25%, Product 19%, Delivery 28%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of PMI's PDF. Relevant text: Domain IV Task 1 'Seek early feedback' ('Deliver work in small increments'; 'Collect and incorporate stakeholders' feedback on a regular basis'); Task 3 'Manage impediments and risk' ('Proactively identify risks and impediments'; 'Prioritize impediment removal and risk mitigation activities'); Domain I Task 7 'Embrace Change' ('Embrace process adaptation by responding to changing requirements and priorities'; 'Adapt to product needs based on the learning and feedback'). The objective wording here is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's sprint-release-before-review-pmiacp (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The company, the product, the team and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You coach a fictional six-person team at Corbel Insurance that maintains the claims portal. The board shows 14 items in progress; few finish each week, and urgent requests arrive daily in chat.
handover: Average cycle time has grown from 4 to 13 days over two months.
Managers message developers directly with 'quick' requests.
howItWorks: The board shows the Sprint's commitments, the work, the impediments, the people's support and the Scrum events.
Move on a day at a time. A decision comes to you at each Daily Scrum; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Day 2: cycle time passes 15 days; a regulatory fix misses its deadline in the review queue.
Day 4: a developer makes a mistake while switching between three requests; claims payments fail for an hour.
Day 8: nobody picks up reviews, which earn no points; nine items sit in review.

wipPrompt.title: Too much started, too little finished

choices.label: Agree WIP limits per column (in progress 4, review 2) and a rule to finish or swarm on blocked items before starting new ones

effects.log: Starting stops; review clears in two days.

choices.feedback: Limiting work in progress reduces queues and switching, so work flows and finishes sooner.

choices.label: Rank the 14 items and keep going
choices.feedback: Clearer order, but everything stays in progress.

choices.label: Start two more urgent items to show responsiveness
Route requests through one intake the product owner orders daily, with one rotating developer handling true urgencies so the others keep focus

effects.log: Direct requests drop to 6 a week.

choices.feedback: Shielding the team from interruptions protects flow; one intake keeps priority decisions with the product owner.

choices.label: Ask developers to mute chat in the mornings

effects.log: Chat is muted in the mornings.

choices.feedback: Fewer interruptions, but requests pile up and arrive in bursts.

choices.label: Accept that responsiveness to managers comes first

metricPrompt.title: Which metric to watch
metricPrompt.context: The manager wants story points per developer.

choices.label: Track cycle time and throughput for the team on a visible chart, review them in retrospectives, and adjust WIP limits from what they show

effects.log: Cycle time falls to 6 days in two weeks.

choices.feedback: Flow metrics such as cycle time and throughput show whether changes improve flow; teams use them to adjust.

choices.label: Track team velocity only
choices.feedback: Velocity says little about how long work waits.

choices.label: Rank developers by story points completed
choices.feedback: People start work they can finish alone and avoid reviews; queues grow.

reflection.question: Write the iteration notes on flow.

parts.label: WIP and interruptions
parts.criteria: Limits of 4 in progress and 2 in review; one intake; rotating responder.
parts.modelAnswer: WIP limits stopped new starts; requests now go through one intake the product owner orders, with one developer on rotation for urgent ones.

parts.label: Metrics
parts.criteria: Cycle time from 13 to 6 days; throughput tracked.
parts.modelAnswer: We track team cycle time and throughput and adjust WIP limits from them; cycle time fell from 13 to 6 days.

scoring.modelReasoning: Flow improves when work in progress is limited, so the team finishes before starting; when the team is shielded from interruptions with one ordered intake; and when flow metrics such as cycle time and throughput, not individual points, guide adjustments.
